A PM is the agent that owns the project: it writes the briefs, dispatches the seats, verifies what comes back and merges it. There is exactly one PM per project.
A seat is one worker agent. It has its own tmux window, its own git worktree and its own session, so two seats never edit the same files.
A worktree is a second checkout of the same repository on its own branch, so a seat can write files while the PM keeps working in the main checkout.
A task branch is the branch a seat's worktree is on. It is named after the task, and it is the evidence of which work belongs to which task.
A brief is the task file under the team's tasks directory. It is the single source of scope and acceptance commands for one task.
The category of a brief is the word after `category:` in its header. The project maps each category to a model, so the category decides which model the seat gets.
A change is a proposal under the project's spec directory that groups the specs a piece of work touches, with its own tasks and its own verification.
A spec is the written contract of one capability: what must hold, as requirements with scenarios. The gate validates the specs, so a spec that does not hold is red.
A gate is the project's own check suite. Green means the checks really ran on this tree; it is evidence only because the same gate fails when the work is broken.
The ledger is the team's written record: the board, the briefs, the threads, the reports and the review records. Agents append to it; the PM owns it.
The pulse is the patrol that wakes the PM on an interval, but only when there is pending work. It runs as a window in the same session.
A knock is the short notification that tells a window there is something to read. It never carries the work itself; the work is in a file.
`--yes` is the explicit authorization a command needs before it changes shared or remote state. Without it the command refuses and writes nothing.

talk to another project's PM

Runs a meeting between this project and another: each side speaks into one shared transcript, and a proposal is only settled when both sides agree to it themselves. It never writes into the other project's repository, and it has no way to give an order: a human is the only one who can carry a decision across projects.
Use it for an interface between two projects, for advice with evidence, or to report a problem that the other side has to know about. It is not a channel for commanding another team.
